**CR-7. Authority model (behaviour).** The host is the sole authority: only a `HOST` kernel ticks and applies; a `MIRROR` never applies. Each command type's owner declares `allowed_origins ⊆ {PLAYER, SYSTEM}` and `actor_binding ∈ {NONE, OWNED_BY_ISSUER}` — both mandatory (CR-6) — and `allowed_origins` is checked at admission, with a P2 re-check as defence in depth. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* A type with `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER` also declares **`actor_source`**: the `block_id` of the registered binding source whose ID space its `actor` belongs to (`body.state` for every avatar-acting type, `emitter.state` for `toggle_beam`). The P2 authority check passes iff `(actor_source(type), actor) ∈ half_b[PlayerId(issuer_peer)]`. So an actor and a beam with the same number can never stand in for each other. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* `SYSTEM` commands never arrive from a network; remote ingress always stamps `PLAYER`. The kernel holds a **binding table** — `peer_id → PlayerId` and `PlayerId → {(source block_id, entity_id)}` — as identity data, not domain state; the table has two halves with different lifetimes *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix; Resolved 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling G6 (user delegated all remaining calls): the kernel owns the rebuild; closes Body Open Question 30)*. **(a) `peer_id → PlayerId`** is session state: it is mutated only through a host-only API called by the session owner (`request_bind_seat(peer_id, player_id)` and `request_unbind_seat(peer_id)`, CR-15) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — ADR-0002 GDD sync)* (a boot step in MVP: `HOST_PEER_ID` 1 → PlayerId 1; Co-op Session in VS-B), and a restore, a death restart or a new game never touches it and never resets any issuer's `seq` or `last_seq`. **(b) `PlayerId → {(source block_id, entity_id)}`** *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* is derived from saved state and is never saved: **the kernel rebuilds it itself as the last step of every pass through `LOADING`** (`request_restore` and `request_new_game` alike), after the last `post_restore()` and the K-4 hash check and before the `LOADING → RUNNING` transition. The rebuild clears half (b) entirely, then calls each registered **binding source** (CR-6, CR-8) in ascending `block_id` order — with `ctx`, as a pure read of its owner's block, under no `WriteScope`, ending `return ctx.complete()` — which delivers `[(player_id, entity_id)]` in ascending order through `ctx.put`, and binds every pair under the source's own `block_id`: each delivered `(player_id, entity_id)` is stored as `player_id → (source_block_id, entity_id)`. Entity IDs are block-local (CR-8: each owner allocates from its own counter and the kernel allocates none), so the key always carries the source. Equal numbers from two sources (Body actor 1 and Emitter beam 1) are two different keys and never conflict. A key `(source_block_id, entity_id)` delivered for two different PlayerIds, or the same triple `(player_id, source_block_id, entity_id)` delivered twice, is `BINDING_REBUILD_CONFLICT`. A source that reports `ctx.fault` or returns without the sentinel is that source's fault. Either one takes `LOADING → FAULTED` naming the source. The checks compare keys only within one source. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix; registry request: `kernel_binding_table` `half_b`, `errors`, `actor_source`, `referenced_by`)* Because `LOADING` is atomic within one boundary service, the rebuild is not a P6 control-plane request and no command can interleave with it; the P6 rule (Section E) governs session-owner changes to half (a) only. At MVP no binding source's pairs change during `RUNNING`, so no `RUNNING` tick sees an empty or stale half (b); a runtime seat or beam reassignment (VS-B) is a session-owner request honoured at P6 (Open Question 4, the co-op ADR). MVP binding sources: Body's `seat_bindings()` (its `SEAT` rows → `(seat, actor_id)`) and the Emitter's `beam_bindings()` (`(player_id, beam_id)`). Single-player: PlayerId 1 → {(`body.state`, avatar actor_id), (`emitter.state`, beam_id)}. Both numbers may be 1 (two independent counters), and the result is valid. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix. Resolved 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix (G6): keyed by source rather than by namespace-tagged IDs, so Body's and the Emitter's persisted ID formats stay unchanged (G1).)* *(Alternative: Player Controller owns the binding as a block — rejected because the kernel could then not aut

======
**CR-8. State-block registry contract.** An owner registers: `block_id` (unique, namespaced, e.g. `graph.state`); `owner`; `schema_version` (bumped on any serialized-shape change); `class` ∈ {`SIM`, `PERCEPTION_OUT`} (CR-12); `persist` (false = derived, rebuilt after load) and, when true, `persist_scope` ∈ {`WORLD`, `PROFILE`} — `WORLD` blocks live in the world snapshot and roll back on `request_restore`; `PROFILE` blocks (decoded rules, lore, scars: Pillar 5's "never knowledge") live outside it and are never rolled back by a world restore; `scope` ∈ {`SHARED`, `PER_PLAYER` keyed by PlayerId}; `gameplay` (bool, mandatory: true when a gameplay verb can change the block; false only for settings, menu and save-request state — the CR-16 paused-write test) and `interpolated` (bool, default false: when true the kernel calls the owner's `commit_baseline()` at P4 so the previous/current pair rolls exactly once per tick, and after a restore or an owner-declared teleport/reset the owner calls `snap_baseline(key)` so presentation never interpolates across a discontinuity) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*; `repl_hint` ∈ {`HOST_ONLY`, `SHARED_SUMMARY`, `OWNER_PRIVATE`} — mandatory now though unused until VS-B, so no block ever ships without the decision; `snapshot(ctx)` (delivers its plain data through `ctx.put(payload)` and ends with `return ctx.complete()`; canonical state only, deterministic ordering, entity references by stable ID, no derived caches; **the payload is a deep copy** — `duplicate_deep()` for Dictionary/Array, `duplicate()` for Packed arrays, which GDScript passes by reference — never a reference into live state); `restore(data, stored_version, ctx)` (whole-block replace; **copies into the existing block object**, so the long-lived `read_view` facade stays valid, and never retains a reference to `data`, so two restores from one payload cannot alias; the owner migrates from `stored_version`; an unsupported version is a reported failure through the fault channel, never a silent default) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*; `default_state(ctx)` (when a save lacks the block; `ctx.put(state)`); `post_restore(ctx)` (after *all* blocks restore: resolve cross-block IDs, rebuild caches, check invariants); `read_view(ctx)` (called once at the registry freeze; delivers through `ctx.put(view)` a long-lived getter-only facade over the block object, never a live container, CR-12; the owner also supplies `empty_view(ctx)`, a facade of the same class whose getters return neutral values and whose `is_empty()` is true) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — ADR-0003 GDD sync)*; `commit_baseline(ctx)` and `snap_baseline(key, ctx)` for `interpolated` blocks; optionally `init_world(world_seed, ctx)` (a new-game step, CR-18); optionally `binding_source(ctx)` (delivers `[(player_id, entity_id)]` ascending through `ctx.put`; read only by the kernel's `LOADING` binding rebuild, CR-7) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*. **Every one of these is a kernel-invoked owner callable, so every one receives `ctx`, returns only `ctx.complete()`'s token, and is never `-> void`** (CR-19(a)/(b)) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R3)*. Restore order follows declared `restore_after`; a cycle in it, or a reference to an unregistered block, fails boot. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* Entity IDs are allocated by the owning block from a counter stored inside it; the kernel allocates none. An ID is therefore unique only within its block. Every cross-block reference the kernel holds (the binding table, CR-7) is keyed `(block_id, entity_id)`, and the kernel assumes no global ID space. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* **No global RNG in simulation**: each system draws from a named stream whose counter lives in its block; the kernel supplies a pure derivation helper from `(world_seed, stream_name, counter)` and, for threat draws only, the epoch-keyed variant `rng_derive_epoch` (D.10) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R1)*. The kernel's own clock (`kernel.clock`: tick counter + world seed, read through a view that also exposes `restore_epoch`) is its one registered block, class `SIM`, `persist = true` (scope `WORLD`; carried in the kernel snapshot payload as `T` and `world_seed`), **never marked dirty and never notifying** (`T` advances every tick; presentation reads it from the batch's `tick` and the read view), and excluded from the D.12 block fold because the hash prefix already cover

======
**CR-18. Snapshot semantics.** A snapshot is taken only at a tick boundary (P6), covers all `persist` blocks at the same T, and records `(T, per-block schema_version)`. Capture is synchronous and in memory with the tick halted (`SAVING`), and **atomic within a single boundary service — `SAVING` never spans a frame**; file I/O is Save/Load's and off the critical path → ADR. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* Restore replaces all `WORLD`-scoped persisted blocks atomically and leaves `PROFILE`-scoped blocks untouched (Pillar 5: losing the ship or a body never loses knowledge); partial restore within a scope is unsupported; failure aborts to `FAULTED` with pre-restore state intact where possible. With join-in-progress deferred, the same snapshot/restore contract is VS-B's guest transfer at session start, so it must be complete and cheap. **New game (K-2):** a new game passes through `LOADING`: every block takes `default_state()`, Save/Load's `new_game(world_seed)` sets `world_seed` into `kernel.clock` *(a new game is entered by the control-plane call `request_new_game(world_seed, restore_epoch = 0)`, valid from `BOOTING` (the first boot, States table), `RUNNING`, `PAUSED` and `FAULTED` *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*, so a second new game in one process — for example "death = restart from the last autosave" when no autosave exists yet — has a path; it flushes the queue with `Dropped(RELOAD)` exactly like `request_restore`, resets `T` to 0, installs the supplied epoch (a fresh slot's `slot_epoch_a/b.bin` pair starts at 0, Save/Load SL-18, SL-23; amended 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling R14) and leaves `PROFILE`-scoped blocks untouched: Pillar 5, a new world never loses knowledge; what a new crew keeps is Open Question 13, Save/Load's) (Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*, then each owner that registered an `init_world(world_seed, scope, ctx)` step runs it in `restore_after` order under one shared `INIT` `WriteScope` that it receives, before `post_restore()`; dirty keys marked under the `INIT` and `RESTORE` scopes are discarded and replaced by one `ALL` batch per block on `LOADING → RUNNING` *(Amended 2026-10-28 — ADR-0003 GDD sync)*; at MVP the world build is Web Map & Transit's `init_world` (WM-7), which calls the Layout, Graph and Body mutators in its fixed order *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from save-load-and-versioned-format (SL-18) and web-map-and-transit)*. The last step of every pass through `LOADING`, restore or new game, is the CR-7 binding rebuild (after the `init_world` steps and `post_restore()`, and after a restore's K-4 hash check), so the first `RUNNING` tick already sees the rebuilt `PlayerId → {(block_id, entity_id)}` half *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*.

| `LOADING` | Restore, `default_state`, `init_world` or `post_restore` fails, or a pre-check fails (`RESTORE_UNKNOWN_BLOCK`, `TICK_RATE_MISMATCH`, `RESTORE_EPOCH_RANGE`), or the binding rebuild reports a conflict or a binding-source fault (`BINDING_REBUILD_CONFLICT`, CR-7) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* | `FAULTED` | Previous state preserved if possible (pre-check failures only) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)* |

======
- **If any block's `post_restore()` fails (cross-block ID unresolved, invariant violated)**: `LOADING → FAULTED` with the block and invariant named. Because restore is whole-block replace and all blocks have been replaced by the time `post_restore` runs, **pre-restore state is not intact here** — "where possible" in CR-18 means pre-check failures only. *(Option)*: capture an in-memory snapshot of the live state before a mid-session restore so diagnostics can diff; automatic revert to it is out of scope (would need a second restore pass that could itself fail).

======
| `LOADING` | Restoring a snapshot or building new-game state; also entered mid-session for reload, including the MVP death stub (Save/Load); entered from `BOOTING` by the first-boot `request_new_game` / `request_restore` *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*. Atomic within one boundary service — it never spans a frame *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. No wait on Save/Load I/O happens inside it: when a restore advances `restore_epoch`, Save/Load's `slot_epoch_a/b.bin` write completes (or is declared not durable) in a pre-restore staging step before `request_restore` is made, and a carried Continue writes nothing (CR-15) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling R14)*. Its last step is the CR-7 binding rebuild *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* | No | No (`NOT_ACCEPTING`) |

======
| `LOADING` | All blocks restored, `post_restore` passes and the CR-7 binding rebuild completes (a new game runs it after the `init_world` steps and `post_restore()`) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* | `RUNNING` | Always `RUNNING` (K-4: Save/Load does not restore into `PAUSED`); a caller that wants `PAUSED` queues `request_pause`, served at the next boundary before any tick runs. The driver clears its accumulator on this transition (CR-1a) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* |

======
**CR-15. Control plane** (host-local, not commands): `request_pause`, `request_resume`, `request_snapshot`, `request_restore`, `request_new_game` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review; CR-18)*, `request_shutdown`, `request_bind_seat(peer_id, player_id)` and `request_unbind_seat(peer_id)` (the host-only writers of binding half (a), CR-7; the composition root calls `request_bind_seat(HOST_PEER_ID, 1)` as a boot step) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — ADR-0002 GDD sync)*. Callers: Save/Load, the pause/Chart Table UI (host-local call), boot code. **Timing** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*: a request is recorded when made — from any phase, from a hook, from a P5 handler, or from outside a tick (a UI call between frames) — and served at the **next boundary**, where a boundary is the P6 of a tick or the driver's per-frame boundary service (run before any tick of the frame and, while `PAUSED`, every frame), whichever comes first; the call itself never changes state. `request_shutdown` is accepted from **every state except `SHUTTING_DOWN`** (including `BOOTING`, `LOADING` and `SAVING`; in those it is served at the boundary that follows the atomic step). Requests reaching the same boundary are applied in arrival order, never coalesced: a `request_pause` then a `request_resume` on one boundary leaves the kernel `RUNNING` with no paused service cycle run; a caller that needs a definite state re-issues the state it wants (Chart Table CT-4) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from chart-table-web-map-and-menus (ASK-CT-9))*. **`request_restore(payload, restore_epoch, expected_state_hash, has_expected_hash)`** (K-4; `has_expected_hash` is a typed `bool` and `0` is a legal hash, so there is no sentinel value) *(Amended 2026-10-29 — ADR-0002 sync)* *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R1; amended 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling R1 as amended by R13/R14: `restore_epoch` is supplied by Save/Load, whose epoch staging step has completed before the call is made: `EPOCH_DURABLE`, or a logged `SL_EPOCH_NOT_DURABLE` with `save_status = FAILED`, or no advance was due. Save/Load advances the value on every death-stub restore, every `FAULT_RECOVERY` and every Continue except one of the newest non-demoted verified `QUIT` generation, which carries it unchanged and writes nothing (R13). The kernel never waits on that write: no Save/Load I/O completes inside `LOADING`, which stays atomic within one boundary service (States). **Listed exposure (failure path, R14):** after `SL_EPOCH_NOT_DURABLE` the installed epoch exists only in Save/Load's memory, so a process kill before Save/Load's next successful epoch write may replay that epoch once; G3/G4 are unaffected because they are defined given the `(save bytes, restore_epoch)` pair. The kernel holds it read-only for the session, exposes it in the `kernel.clock` read view (CR-8) and rejects a value outside the u32 range in its pre-check, `RESTORE_EPOCH_RANGE`)*: when `has_expected_hash` is true, the kernel recomputes `state_hash(PERSIST, T)` (D.12) after the last `post_restore()`, inside `LOADING` and before the first `RUNNING` tick, and reports the K-4 verdict `{T, computed_hash, verdict}` to the requester, `verdict` one of `MATCH`, `MISMATCH` or `NONE`; when `has_expected_hash` is false (the pre-K-4 release file case) the compare is skipped, `expected_state_hash` is ignored and the verdict is `NONE` *(Amended 2026-10-29 — ADR-0002 sync)*. **Acyclicity argument.** Restore order: `layout.state` (root, `restore_after: []`) → `graph.state` (`restore_after: [layout.state]`) → `body.state` (`restore_after: [layout.state]`, BDY, designed) → `emitter.state` (`restore_after: [layout.state, graph.state, body.state, controller.state]`) → `interaction.state` (`restore_after: [layout.state, controller.state, graph.state, body.state, emitter.state]`, IA-36, designed; IA-36 lists `body.state` directly because IA-37's `post_restore` reads restored body positions, and the chain `layout.state -> graph.state -> body.state -> emitter.state -> interaction.state` is unchanged in order, so the argument holds *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*; *amended 2026-10-27 — re-review: was "in flight"*). Layout reads no other block in `restore()`; its cross-block reads (the Graph's `area`, Item DB `def_id`s) happen only in `post_restore` and in P3, after every `restore()` has completed. The Layout ↔ Graph data-level mutuality (Layout calls M1; the Graph keys compartments by `room_id`) is therefore never a restore cycle. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*
====
(c) *Class 2 — leaf-dependent results, valid only after Layout's own `post_restore()`.* DOOR_LEAF rects depend on the Graph's persisted `area`, which Layout cannot read inside its own `restore()` (the Graph restores after Layout) and which the Graph now publishes as `opening(edge_id) -> {area, area_max, door_state}` (LY-10; the ask is closed, OQ-3). *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* **(orchestrator ruling; routed amendment to the Layout-side promise "every query is valid immediately after restore":)** leaves are derived by one `derive_doors` pass in Layout's `post_restore` (the kernel guarantees every `restore()` has completed before any `post_restore()` begins, KRN:843, so the Graph's persisted `area` is in memory whatever the order of the `post_restore` calls) and thereafter by `layout.doors`. Between `restore()` and `post_restore()` leaf-dependent queries (`rects_in`, `solid_in`, `clip_to_footprints`, `leaf_would_overlap`, `door_passage` (reports `open_extent_px` 0) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*) report the TEMPLATE default (every leaf closed) and raise a `stale_leaf` diagnostic flag if read. **Self-heal:** Layout's `post_restore` bumps `version(section_id)` (1 → 2) for every section whose derived leaf set differs from the all-closed template default; LY-12(d)'s "a restore is an unconditional rebuild signal" and the Emitter's W0 `version` read (EM:227) therefore rebuild the Emitter's static layer on tick 1 with no ordering between the two `post_restore` calls, and `body.integrate after: layout.doors` (LY-10) covers every P3 reader. Whether `post_restore` order follows `restore_after` is **informational only** (CR-8 and KRN:843 say "after every `restore()`"); no Layout rule depends on the answer. The `stale_leaf` diagnostic and this restore path are **live behaviour**, not a stand-in for an unanswered ask: they stay as specified now that the Graph read exists, because the window between `restore()` and `post_restore()` is real whatever the Graph publishes. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* `post_restore` also bumps `leaf_version` (never `static_version`) for each such section, and rebuilds the derived `opening_leaves` map from the restored `welds[]` and `seam_view(seam_id).opening_ids[]`.

### 7. Snapshot, restore and `post_restore`

**7.1 Snapshot.** `GraphSnapshot.build(state, out)` walks `GraphSchema` and, for each table and column, places `column.duplicate()` into the nested Dictionary, then `ctx.put(payload)`. It reads nothing but `GraphState`, includes no derived or diagnostic member, and the same payload feeds `canonical_encode` (the kernel encodes; the Graph has no byte writer, ADR-0005 § 3.1). A snapshot may be taken on any tick, which is why the queues, `draw_grant`, hook cursors and hysteresis memory are persisted.

**7.2 Restore** (`GraphRestore.restore(data, stored_version, ctx)`, two-phase, ADR-0006 § 2.2). Phase 1 decodes `data` into a fresh scratch `GraphState` (every column `duplicate()`d out of `data`, no reference kept into it) and validates it. Phase 2, on success only, assigns the scratch columns into the live `GraphState` member by member (the object is never replaced, so facades stay valid) and calls `GraphDerived.reset_caches()` (the one cache write `graph_restore.gd` triggers, performed by the cache writer file). Any failure is `ctx.fault(GraphFaults.RESTORE_<name>, detail)` with the live state untouched; there is no clamp and no partial apply. **Validation runs in a fixed order and the first failure wins**, so a given corrupt input always yields the same reason (the 1,000-mutation fuzz of the GDD depends on it):

| Step | Check | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `stored_version` is 1 | `RESTORE_BAD_VERSION(stored, supported)` |
| 2 | exact table and column key sets (and `hdr` keys), `String` keys, expected element types | `RESTORE_BAD_TAG(key)` |
| 3 | all columns of a table have the same length; CSR runs (`ports`, seam lists, `defs`) lie inside their arrays | `RESTORE_BAD_LENGTH(field, expected, got)` |
| 4 | enum columns lie in their `GraphIds` domain | `RESTORE_BAD_ENUM(field, slot, value)` |
| 5 | numeric columns lie in `[min, max]` of their `GraphSchema` spec, including the hard ceilings `max_stock_*`; flag bytes use only defined bits; canonical zeros hold | `RESTORE_OUT_OF_RANGE(field, slot, value)`; a zero violation is `RESTORE_INVARIANT(canonical_zero)` |
| 6 | ids strictly ascending in nodes, edges, seams, sections | `RESTORE_ID_ORDER(slot)` |
| 7 | each `next_*` is above every id in its table | `RESTORE_COUNTER(counter, max_id)` |
| 8 | every live edge endpoint names a live node; no live edge points at a tombstone | `RESTORE_BAD_EDGE_ENDPOINT(edge_id)` |
| 9 | every seam sub-edge has its SeamRecord and every record's lists name rows of the right kind | `RESTORE_SEAM_MISMATCH(seam_id)` |
| 10 | queue lengths within bounds, queue subjects name live rows | `RESTORE_QUEUE(queue, length)` |
| 11 | every `defs` entry the nodes reference is known to the catalog (`ItemCatalog.has`) | `RESTORE_UNKNOWN_DEF(def_id)` |
| 12 | any LS-24 structural check not named above | `RESTORE_INVARIANT(name)` |

**7.3 Out-of-range is hard, a cap tuning drift is not (resolves TR-itemdb-033 against LS-21).** Step 5's maxima are **physical hard ceilings** from `GraphTuning` (the `n_max(c)` of a room is checked in `post_restore`, § 7.4, because it needs `V`; a store's hard ceiling is `max_stock_*`), not the catalog's tunable `stock_cap`. A save whose store content exceeds a **lowered live `stock_cap`** is therefore valid: it restores byte-identically (so `snapshot(restore(snapshot()))` still holds and no REBASED cause is needed), and the **stock reconcile**, which runs at the head of every phase 0, clamps `stock` to the live cap, credits the excess to the section's `disc_*` counter (conservation closes), increments `GraphDiag.stock_clamped` (a legal event, **not** a saturation, so the all-zero saturations assertion stands) and emits a diagnostic naming node, old stock and cap. In steady state the reconcile is a no-op loop over the stores. The reconcile is a function of persisted state and the frozen catalog only, so replay stays deterministic. ADR-0016 shares this row and may prefer the clamp in `post_restore`; this ADR chooses phase 0 because it keeps the restore byte-identical (Open Question 2). A `gdd_sync` item carves the case out of LS-21's "never by clamping".

**7.4 `post_restore`** (`GraphDerived.post_restore(ctx)`, runs after Layout's restore because of `restore_after`): **(1)** for each compartment row, look up `room_ref` through the `RoomSource` port; an unknown room is `RESTORE_UNKNOWN_ROOM(room_ref)` for the first such compartment (loud by design, no default `V`); **(2)** check `n_o2 + n_inert` against `P_MAX x V x GAS_SCALE` per compartment, `RESTORE_OUT_OF_RANGE("n_gas", slot, value)`; **(3)** rebuild every DERIVED cache (`ensure_derived()`, including `served_pm`, intensive values and the descriptor store, writing no persisted field and drawing no RNG); **(4)** seed the last-emitted buckets from the restored values and the band and STRAIN memory from the payload (never re-derived from the values), so the first run reproduces an uninterrupted run and the kernel's one `ALL` batch is followed by silence (ADR-0012 owns the phase code that reads the seeds); **(5)** run the structural invariants of LS-24 in every build. Cross-block verifiers (INV-x) and the order among blocks' `post_restore` are ADR-0016's. A fault here fails the whole load (kernel `LOADING` to `FAULTED`), because `post_restore` runs after the swap; ADR-0016 must guarantee a faulted `LOADING` never enters play with the restored world (cross-ADR assumption).

**7.5 Versioning.** `schema_version` is 1 and `supported_versions` is `[1]`. A future shape change registers a pure `(old Dictionary) -> new Dictionary` migration in `graph_restore.gd` and bumps both the version and the committed schema fingerprint in the same commit; retained golden saves in `tests/fixtures/saves/` are migration fixtures (TR-lsg-040, ADR-0006 § 2.6).

### 8. Faults

**8.1 Domain 3 table** (`src/sim/graph/graph_faults.gd`, `class_name GraphFaults`, `DOMAIN_ID = 3`, codes pre-packed `(DOMAIN_ID << 16) | local`, append-only, never reused; `NAMES` indexed by local code):

| Local | Name | Raised when |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `NOT_IN_SCOPE` | (ADR-0003 § 6's example, kept) a mutator defect that is not the plain `REFUSED` |
| 2 | `RESTORE_BAD_VERSION` | § 7.2 step 1 |
| 3 | `RESTORE_BAD_TAG` | step 2 |
| 4 | `RESTORE_BAD_LENGTH` | step 3 |
| 5 | `RESTORE_BAD_ENUM` | step 4 |

content.thinking:
I'm noting that ADR-0011 and ADR-0016 share TR-itemdb-033, where ADR-0011 already settled on a phase-0 reconcile approach: when a restored store's saved stock exceeds a lowered live stock_cap, it clamps to the cap, pushes the excess into disc_*, closes conservation, and emits a diagnostic.

Now I'm weighing whether ADR-0016 should accept that clamping happens outside restore/post_restore, at the first phase-0 hook afterward, versus clamping inside post_restore itself. Clamping in post_restore would violate the rule that post_restore must not mutate persisted state, would cause a state_hash mismatch leading to a REBASED verdict, and would break restore idempotence, so I'm settling on accepting ADR-0011's approach and establishing that post_restore only ever writes derived state, with no exceptions — the stock reconcile stays a hook-time clamp outside that boundary.

Beyond that, I'm working out the failure path: any restore failure must force the kernel into FAULTED, where it never ticks, never autosaves, and never touches persisted state, with the half-restored blocks marked poisoned and surfaced via a LoadFailure diagnostic record; recovery can only happen through request_restore or new_game, which fully rebuild the WORLD blocks, and the save/load system should treat this as RESTORE_FAILED, incrementing quarantine counts and falling back to the prior candidate generation.

I'm considering whether to add an in-memory rollback before restoring, but the GDD puts that out of scope, so I'm rejecting automatic revert. Instead I'm thinking in terms of a staged kernel-level process — restore each block internally via scratch-then-commit, then run post_restore in DAG order, then verifiers, then a hash comparison, then rebind — while recognizing that once the first block commits, the pre-restore state is no longer intact, but that only matters for mid-session failures, and in MVP there's nothing live worth preserving in those cases (death-stub restore has no player state to save, and Continue-from-menu has nothing live either), so this gap is acceptable for now.

My conclusion is that pre-check failures stay clean and leave state intact, while owner restore/post_restore failures intentionally don't, since Save/Load just retries with a fresh LOADING pass against the next candidate. To keep this cheap, the kernel halts the whole pass the moment any block's restore faults, moves to FAULTED, and emits a structured LoadFailure with phase, block ID, code, and detail. I'm also weighing whether to offer a dry-run validation step but deciding against the added cost, and refining the rule that restore() may only read predecessor blocks' already-committed restored state through read views — not derived caches that need post_restore — which is why Body's BDY_RESTORE_UNKNOWN_BODY check against Layout's restored state is valid, since Layout's static queries become valid immediately after its own restore completes.

Since read views are long-lived facades grabbed at setup time rather than per-call, the kernel can't intercept individual reads to catch violations dynamically, so enforcement has to fall to static lint checks on declared dependencies plus a fuzz test that restores a snapshot under multiple random valid topological orderings and checks for identical state hashes — a good way to catch undeclared ordering dependencies.

For the tie-break rule itself, I'm weighing registration-index order (matching ADR-0003's hook convention) against ascending block_id order. I'll go with block_id ascending bytewise comparison since it's independent of composition-root ordering and stays reproducible even if registration order changes, matching how binding sources are already rebuilt.

Now I'm tracing through the actual dependency graph to verify this works: starting with roots like layout.state, sanity.state, and suit.state, then working through graph.state, body.state, controller.state, and the more deeply nested states like emitter.state, interaction.state, assembly.state, web.state, attention.state, and horror.state to confirm the topological order resolves consistently with id-based tie-breaking.

I'm checking the total block count — layout, graph, body, controller, emitter, suit, interaction, assembly, web, attention, horror, sanity.state, sanity.ledger plus kernel.clock should total 14, matching SL-19's persisted block requirement. I'm also verifying there's no cycle risk between suit and controller's restore_after dependencies, and considering whether a new kernel error code like RESTORE_CYCLE is needed to handle cycle detection in restore_after chains, distinct from the existing HOOK_CYCLE code.

Now I'm working through edge cases: self-referencing restore_after entries counting as cycles, duplicate entries triggering descriptor errors, and whether restore_after edges to non-persisted blocks are even meaningful. I'm concluding that non-persisted blocks still need post_restore to rebuild derived state, which means the dependency DAG actually has to include blocks like sanity.perception even though they don't persist — their post_restore pulls from sanity.state after reload.

I'm also sorting out the WORLD vs PROFILE scope distinction: during an in-session restore, only WORLD blocks get restore/post_restore, while PROFILE blocks are left untouched since there are zero PROFILE blocks at MVP anyway. For a cold boot, though, both scopes load together, so PROFILE blocks would get restore and post_restore in the same pass. I'm deciding that post_restore should be mandatory for every block (even as a no-op stub) and that default_state applies universally for new games, and now I'm starting to lay out the actual loading pass algorithm with its RESTORE and NEW_GAME pass kinds, beginning with the common step of flushing the queue.

Working through the RESTORE pass pre-checks now — unknown block IDs, header tick rate mismatches, epoch range violations, and schema version compatibility. I'm realizing ADR-0003's code list doesn't actually cover an unsupported stored schema version case, which seems like a gap that needs flagging to the foundation team, since the kernel's version check would just be a backstop behind Save/Load's earlier validation. I'm also puzzling over how the kernel would even know the saved tick rate, since that info seems to live in Save/Load's header rather than the kernel's payload — maybe it's embedded in the `kernel.clock` payload entry.

Now I want to verify this against ADR-0006 §3.6, so I'm planning to grep for tick_rate references across ADR-0005 and ADR-0006 to confirm the payload structure. I'm also working out how default_state behaves when a save is missing a block — it seems like default_state(ctx) might construct a default payload dictionary that the kernel then feeds into restore(), rather than mutating the block directly, so I want to check ADR-0011 §4.6 to confirm how this is actually implemented.

| 5 | `LAYOUT_RESTORE_COUNTER` | restore: a counter not equal to the dense count + 1, a non-dense id column |
| 6 | `LAYOUT_RESTORE_DANGLING` | restore and post-restore: a weld, socket or body reference that does not resolve; an `area` above `area_max` found in `post_restore` |
| 7 | `LAYOUT_OFFSET_OFF_GRID` | defect in LM2 apply |
| 8 | `LAYOUT_COMPONENT_COUNT` | defect in LM3 apply |
| 9 | `LAYOUT_APPLY_PRECONDITION` | defect: an apply reached without its check having passed |

Content boot errors stay in domain 2 (ADR-0007 § 2.3); Layout raises none of them from its own faults file. Diagnostics (counters, not faults): `opening_unknown`, `opening_invalid`, `area_clamped`, `stale_leaf`, `query_box_empty`, `geometry_changed_fresh`, `visual_changed`, `hatch_one_sided`, `layout_block_soft_bytes`, registered as one diagnostics channel (field list ADR-0031's).

**Key space.** `KeySpaceDescriptor` for `layout.state`: kinds `[1, 2, 3, 4]` named `[SEC, BODY, SEAM, LEAF]`, no events, `quiet_writes_allowed = false` (every discrete change marks a key; the per-mutator fixture asserts the specific keys). Keys are integers `(KIND << 32) | id` through `DirtyKey.make`; the worst MVP count (6) is far under `MAX_DIRTY_KEYS`.

**Order of writes inside a mutator.** Every mutator begins `scope.open_for(&"layout.state")`; on `false` it writes nothing and returns `REFUSED`. It then computes the full result (ids, offsets, components, slot sets) into locals and the `out` object **before** its first write to `LayoutState`, writes the columns, updates `LayoutDerived`, bumps counters, and marks keys last. A packed-array element write never relies on a setter (4.7).

**Hash and cadence.** `layout_hash()` calls the kernel `block_hash(&"layout.state")` (ADR-0005 § 5.3), memoised on `mutation_count`, a non-persisted counter bumped by LM1 to LM4 and reset to 0 by `restore()` with the memo invalidated; it is never computed per tick. The comparison with Save/Load's stored `block_state_hash` after restore is a diagnostic only.

### 10. Restore, drift and `post_restore`

**`restore(data, stored_version, ctx)` is two-phase** (ADR-0003 § 2, ADR-0006 § 2.2): decode and validate into a `LayoutScratch` (cold path, allocation allowed); on any failure call `ctx.fault(code, detail)` and write nothing; on success **copy the contents into the existing `LayoutState` object** (each column assigned from the scratch's own arrays, none aliasing `data`), then rebuild the static `LayoutDerived` (lookups, socket index, caps, version counters reset to 1, `mutation_count` 0, memo cleared, broadphase handles rebuilt by ADR-0014's call). A restore swaps whole tables only on success (TR-section-007).

**Validation, in order** (first failure wins, with a named detail): (1) `stored_version` in `supported_versions` and the key set equals the § 2 table, every column has the declared type and equal row counts per table (`LAYOUT_RESTORE_SCHEMA`); (2) every `template_id` resolves in the catalog (`LAYOUT_RESTORE_UNKNOWN_TEMPLATE`); (3) `rot_q` all 0 (`LAYOUT_ROT_UNSUPPORTED`); (4) the drift policy below (`LAYOUT_RESTORE_TEMPLATE_CHANGED`); (5) dense ids: `section_id[i] == i + 1`, `body_id[i] == i + 1`, `room_id_base[i + 1] == room_id_base[i] + rooms(template[i])`, counters equal the dense count + 1 and below the ceilings (`LAYOUT_RESTORE_COUNTER`); (6) references: every non-discarded instance sits on a `LIVE` body, every `LIVE` body has an in-range `origin_section_id` that belongs to it, socket rows are strictly ascending with `socket_index < template.socket_count` and a resolving `seam_id`, weld rows ascend and agree with their socket states (`ACTIVE` with two `WELDED`, `CUT_SEALED` with two `CAPPED`, `CUT_RAGGED` with two `CUT_OPEN`), `ACTIVE` welds form a forest whose components are exactly the `LIVE` bodies' section sets, and every `ACTIVE` weld's offsets satisfy `offset_b = offset_a + pos_a - pos_b` on the 24 grid (`LAYOUT_RESTORE_DANGLING`). An unsupported `stored_version` is a reported failure, never a silent default.

**Drift policy (TR-section-007).** The current template's three hashes are compared with the stored ones after `& 0xFFFFFFFF`. A **`structure_hash`** difference is `LAYOUT_RESTORE_TEMPLATE_CHANGED` for every instance (§ 4). A **`geometry_hash`** difference is `LAYOUT_RESTORE_TEMPLATE_CHANGED` when the instance carries history, meaning any non-`FREE` socket, any `welds[]` row naming it, or a body shared with another section, because a moved socket or wall edge under a welded or cut instance restores with broken abutment; on a never-welded `FREE` instance alone it is accepted with the diagnostic `geometry_changed_fresh`, the rects are re-derived from the new template and the stored hash is rewritten. A **`visual_hash`** difference alone is accepted with `visual_changed` and rewritten. A hash collision cannot hide a structural change that also changes a tile set or key sequence in a way the validation of step (6) detects; a 2^-32 collision on `structure_hash` is accepted and recorded (§ Risks R6). Pre-release saves are disposable; after the first outside build the migration obligation of LY-6 e applies, and a rewritten hash means the next snapshot differs from the stored one, so the K-4 `state_hash` compare reports a mismatch as a diagnostic, as designed.

**Query validity after restore.** Class 1 (static, valid when `restore()` returns): `room_at`, `V`, `exposed_tiles`, `room_surface`, `socket_plan`, `anchor_geometry`, static rect membership, `section_offset`, `body_of`, `section_at`. Class 2 (leaf-dependent, valid after `post_restore()`): `rects_in`/`solid_in` door leaves, `clip_to_footprints`, `leaf_would_overlap`, `door_passage_into`. Between the two they report the template default (every leaf closed) and raise `stale_leaf` if read; `LayoutDerived.leaves_valid` is the flag. The kernel guarantees every `restore()` completes before any `post_restore()` begins.

**`post_restore(ctx)`** (a) runs one `derive_doors` pass over the leaf cache using `opening_into` (an `area` above `area_max` is clamped with a diagnostic, and the same fault found *here* is `LAYOUT_RESTORE_DANGLING`; an unknown opening leaves the leaf closed); (b) rebuilds `opening_leaves` from the restored `welds[]` and `seam_openings_into`; (c) bumps `version` and `leaf_version` (never `static_version`) for each section whose derived leaf set differs from the all-closed default, so a restored open door is a 1 to 2 transition and every rebuilding consumer rebuilds on tick 1 with no ordering between `post_restore` calls; (d) runs cross-block **verification** through `section_counts_into`: every `graph_ref_base` resolves (node, edge and compartment counts match the template), every `welds[]` `seam_id` resolves to a Graph seam record, and `graph.next_section_id == layout.next_section_id`. Failures use the restore codes. Verification order and the "installed `def_id` at a hardpoint resolves" diagnostic belong to ADR-0016's verifier list; this ADR supplies the checks Layout's side can run. After a restore every section reports `changed_region` ALL once, and the kernel delivers one `ALL` batch (ADR-0003 § 4).

**Policy line (TR-derelict-008 Layout half).** A save restores from its **saved values**: templates are never mutated at runtime, a restore never re-templates an instance, and no Authoring content lint runs at restore.

### 11. Read views: records, tiers, order and frames

Reads are pure, side-effect free, deterministic and identical before a snapshot and after restoring it (idempotent), and have **no "perceived" variant** (Pillar 1, TR-section-039). They are exposed through the long-lived `LayoutViews` facade (ADR-0003 § 7); no live container is ever returned. Two tiers:

- **Tier H (hot; allocation-free; tagged `## @hot` for ADR-0010 `HOT-01`; scalar results or caller-owned `out`):** `room_at(section_id, x, y) -> int` (`0` = NONE; a sill px answers its `sill_room`, so no walkable point answers NONE), `floor_tile_at(...) -> int` (`-1` = NONE), `section_at(body_id, x, y) -> int` (`0` = NONE; FLOOR division), `section_offset_x/_y(section_id)`, `body_of(section_id)`, `version`, `static_version`, `leaf_version`, `changed_region_kind/_box_into`, `door_passage_into`, `leaf_would_overlap`, `leaf_obstruction_into`, `V(room_id)`, `exposed_tiles(room_id)`, and ADR-0014's `rects_in`/`solid_in` (sentinels for an unknown or discarded section are `0`/false, never an error).
- **Tier C (cold; may allocate; returns a freshly built immutable record or a typed `Array[Record]`):** `room_surface`, `room_boundary`, `anchor_geometry`, `subject_anchors`, `socket_plan`, `weld_offset`, `detach_preview`, `room_adjacency`, `hull_segments_near`, `loose_slots`, `hardpoints_of`, `segment_at`, `plate_positions`, `sections_of`, `route_length_px`, `south_band`, `wall_face_rows`, `template_hash`.

**Fixed field names, orders and bounds.** Records live in `src/sim/layout/views/` as get-only `RefCounted` classes: `AnchorGeometry {kind, host_face_id, base_px_polyline (PackedInt32Array pairs), sort_origin_y, section_id}`, `RoomSurface {floor_tiles (PackedInt32Array pairs, tile id ascending), wall_faces}` (the Failure & Trail contract, section-local), `DoorPassage` (D.5 table), `RoomAdjacencyRow {room_a, room_b_or_exterior, via (DOOR|HATCH), via_id, sill_room}`, `SubjectAnchor {local_key, kind_hint, anchor_px, room_id, console_role}`. Ordering contracts: `room_adjacency` by `(room_a, via_id)`; `subject_anchors` and the slot reads by key ascending; `plate_positions` by HULL_SEGMENT node id ascending; `room_surface` by tile id; `sections_of` by `section_id`; `detach_preview` by `section_id`. `wall_face_rows` returns at most 16 rows (the Failure & Trail bound `WALL_ROWS_MAX`). Cold reads that depend only on a template (`room_adjacency`, `south_band`, `plate_positions`) are precomputed once per template in the catalog row, so a read is a copy, not a recomputation.

**CONSOLE anchors (TR-derelict-034, re-tagged 2026-10-29).** `subject_anchors(section_id)` returns `SubjectAnchor` rows with `kind_hint` in `{DOOR_FACE, HARDPOINT, SOCKET, SLOT, CONSOLE, INSTRUMENT}`; `console_role` is `POD` or `DOCK` and is **present iff `kind_hint` is `CONSOLE`**. The structural lint `CONSOLE_ROLE_UNSET` (ERROR, boot-tier invariant) rejects a CONSOLE anchor without a role and a role on any other kind. The counts "each dock room holds exactly one dock status glow on its docked-podcraft prop" and "the world holds exactly four CONSOLE anchors" are **Derelict Authoring content lints** (`POD_CONSOLE_MISSING`, `DOCK_CONSOLE_MISSING`, the world-level count) evaluated over this read; Layout asserts no placement and counts nothing at runtime.

**Frame rule (TR-section-039, LY-3 c).** Every geometry read answers section-local base px; the caller composes `section_offset`. Reads that answer for one body answer in the body frame. A read never mixes frames.

### 12. Capacity, size and world-build budgets

- **Ceilings** are the registered constants and GDD knobs named in § 9, loaded from the `LayoutTuning` `ScalarTable` in the default-config data (ADR-0007 § 1.5); the module source contains no literal for any of them, and a start-up test runs the module at each knob's published minimum and maximum. Published ranges are guidance: an out-of-range value appears in the ADVISORY range report and is never clamped or asserted at boot; only schema bounds (`CONTENT_FIELD_RANGE`) and named structural invariants (`CONTENT_INVARIANT`: `area_max > 0`, `GRID_24`, `RECT_STRIDE_OVERFLOW`, `RECT_FLAGS_ILLEGAL`, `CONSOLE_ROLE_UNSET`, rotation 0) refuse a load (TR-section-033 Layout side).
- **Block size.** `bytes ~ 4 * (14 I + 10 K + 4 S + 3 B + 3)` over instance, weld, socket and body rows (D.21 with the 14th column), plus strings; `LAYOUT_BLOCK_SOFT_BYTES` raises the one-shot diagnostic `layout_block_soft_bytes`; `MAX_BLOCK_BYTES` is Save/Load's hard ceiling. The long-campaign shape (24 live and 200 tombstoned sections) is tens of KB.
- **World ceilings (TR-webmap-036 Layout half).** Layout supplies `V(room)` and the rect and door counts; the tile ceiling `TILES_WORLD_MVP`, the S0 to S4 loaded-set tile counts and `INTERACT_FIXTURE_BUDGET` are lints and tests owned by Derelict Authoring and Web Map. A test builds the S4 loaded set through `build_section` (not a hand sum) and asserts the real `V` totals and rect counts against them. `BUILD_TILES_PER_FRAME` (GDD Tuning Knobs) is the PROJECTOR's chunk size (ADR-0034); Layout's contribution is the per-section tile count.

Now I need to figure out for ADR-0016 where cross-block verifiers should live—a central verifier registry versus embedding them in each block's post_restore. I'm leaning toward owner-supplied pure read functions registered as a typed descriptor, but since ADR-0003's registrar lacks a register_verifier hook and BlockDescriptor is fixed, I'm weighing whether verifier logic should instead just live as code inside Assembly's post_restore.

Option B, a dedicated kernel verification phase run after all post_restores complete, seems cleaner since it guarantees derived caches are fully rebuilt before any verifier runs, avoiding ordering issues where one block's check depends on another's unfinished state. But this would require a new registration surface, and it slightly conflicts with the TR documents (TR-section-009, TR-assembly-009), which place verification inside post_restore itself rather than as a separate phase.

With the post_restore ordering following the dependency DAG, Assembly's checks naturally run after Layout, Graph, Interaction, and Body, so its invariant reads stay valid; Layout's checks run earlier but only touch persisted Graph state, which is also fine. That means I don't actually need a new kernel phase or registration surface — verifiers can simply live inside the owning block's post_restore as pure functions reading persisted state of any block and derived state only of declared predecessors. So I'm settling on Decision V1: no separate verification phase, with each verifier implemented as a static function returning a packed result code plus detail output, organized under each block's own verify directory.

I'll keep in mind the rejected alternative of a centralized kernel verification pass — it would unify fault attribution but adds a new registrar surface that's unnecessary given DAG ordering already handles cases like Emitter's static layer rebuild depending on Layout's derived leaves.

The deeper question is whether the post_restore DAG preserves the same topological order as restore itself — I decide yes, one shared ordering for both phases. But that raises a subtlety around Layout's post_restore reading Graph's persisted state through the read-view port: some methods like `opening_into` and `section_counts_into` read purely persisted columns and are safe, but if they hit derived caches like GraphCaches before Graph's own post_restore runs, they'd return stale or empty results. So I need a rule tagging "restore-window reads" as only those answerable from persisted tables, with any premature derived-cache read flagged as `STALE_DERIVED_READ`.

**5.2 Invalidation by the touch serial, not by a dirty key.** ADR-0004 advances `touch_serial[block]` on every granted `scope.open_for(block)` (in `APPLY`, `HOOK`, `PAUSED_APPLY`, `INIT` and `RESTORE` scopes alike). Belt and braces: `restore`, `init_world` and `default_state` do not all open a `WriteScope` the same way (ADR-0003 § 3: `init_world` gets a `WriteScope` (INIT) and a `SnapshotContext`, and `restore` and `post_restore` may write through a RESTORE scope), so the kernel resets the cache entry itself rather than relying on the owner's scope usage; it resets it (`serial = -1`) for every block it replaces on those three calls, independent of the serial. That is a strictly sound "this block may have changed" signal, because every mutator begins with `open_for` (ADR-0003), and it covers the case a dirty key cannot: a quantised write (the Graph's sub-bucket changes, Web Map's marks-nothing leg ticks) changes the hash and marks no key (ADR-0004 § 7, `quiet_writes_allowed`). This ADR therefore adopts the serial in place of the kernel GDD D.12's "invalidated by the block's dirty bit" (and TR-cmd-040's "only by `mark_dirty`"); the cost is that a scope that opens a block and changes nothing also invalidates it, which costs one extra encode at the next cached read and nothing on a tick with no reader. A write outside any scope (no `open_for`, so no serial change) leaves the cache stale; that is the existing `SIM_WRITE_TRIPWIRE` case, is caught by every uncached verification path (KRN-HASH-02, re-targeted to a fixture that writes without a scope) and by the detector in § 5.5. A property setter never invalidates anything (4.7: a packed-array element write skips the setter, P8).

I need to settle on the semantics for default_state myself: when the kernel calls it, the owner resets the block's contents in place to its empty defaults, rather than replacing the object entirely, and then finishes by calling ctx.complete().

I'm leaning toward a unified "default-through-restore" approach instead: the owner calls `ctx.put(payload)` with the current schema version's default payload, and the kernel routes that payload through the same `restore` function used for normal loads. For restore scope, each block's post_restore only touches its own domain, so for Emitter subject re-registration Interaction just verifies against the Emitter read-only, and I need to decide whether a mismatch should trigger a fault or defer reconciliation to the first hook run under ADR-0020.

Since registering is itself a write to Emitter's persisted state and the RESTORE scope forbids writes outside the owning block, I'm deciding re-registration has to happen idempotently: post_restore only reads and compares, and any repair happens in the normal HOOK scope during the first hook run, before emitter.place fires in that same tick. **BDY-31 — Persistence and restore idempotence.** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)* **Snapshot and restore shape, stated once.** `snapshot()` returns plain data (kernel CR-8) and `restore(data, stored_version, ctx)` takes that same shape, decoded by Save/Load, so a restore input is a Variant-shaped tree in which the type check can meet a float or a string: `{next_actor_id: int, n_bodies: int, n_actors: int, bodies: <n_bodies * 6 ints>, actors: <n_actors * 10 ints>}`, flat row-major, rows ascending by id, the body columns in the order `body_id, world_x, world_y, vel_x, vel_y, heading_q` and the actor columns in the order `actor_id, kind, seat, body_id, pos_x, pos_y, sub_x, sub_y, last_octant, odometer`. The canonical BYTES of BDY-32 (3) are the kernel's TLV encoding of exactly this payload (`canonical_encode(snapshot())`, kernel D.12) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*; they are what the hash, the golden file (AC-BDY-110) and the byte-identity claim use, and they are never a restore input. `restore` validates in this order and rejects the WHOLE block at the first failure, leaving the live state untouched: type (every element a plain integer), count, per-row fields, order and canonicity, then Layout liveness. `snapshot(restore(snapshot()))` is byte-identical for `body.state` alone (equal `canonical_encode` output; SL-15 item 10), so `body.state` leaves `REBASE_BLOCKS` (SL:577, "emptied when the Controller/Body owners answer"). `post_restore` sets `pos_prev := pos_curr` (and resets `world_prev := world`, BDY-26) because `pos_prev` is a non-persisted derived field that Body itself must re-derive after a restore (BDY-6; SL-15 item 8 (SL:230)); that write is **Body-internal derivation and is NOT the camera-continuity mechanism**: camera and presentation restore continuity is solely the kernel's `snap_baseline` on entry to `RUNNING` plus the camera CUT on a `PresentationClock.load_seq` change (ADR-0008 § 6.1; ADR-0001 § 4), and Pipeline C5 no longer asks Body for a `post_restore` `previous := current` *(Amended 2026-10-29 — sync knock-on fix: ADR-0008 § 6.1, TD-22)*. It preserves `sub` (it is persisted and is not touched), and verifies the table below. Because Body compares the move octant with its OWN persisted `last_octant` (BDY-12), a key still held across a restore reads N versus N, no change, and the residue continues; a key released during the save/load window reads NONE versus N and resets `sub` exactly as a stop does in uninterrupted play. 106:There is no `Kernel` autoload and no static singleton for kernel or game state. The main scene's root script (the **composition root**, `src/game/game.gd`) constructs the kernel, the `TickDriver` and the `KernelHost`, then gives every module and subscriber **the narrowest facet it needs through `setup()`**, never the whole `Kernel`: a simulation module receives the registration and mutator-scope services ADR-0003
123:│               1 boundary service (SAVING/LOADING/pause/resume; may clear acc, discard this frame's delta;
124:│                 on LOADING → RUNNING: load_seq += 1, then deliver_all; snap_baseline on entry to RUNNING)
178:	get: return _kernel_load_seq()                 # +1 by the kernel on every LOADING -> RUNNING (restore and new game), immediately before deliver_all; never on PAUSED/SAVING -> RUNNING

I'm trying to figure out how Save/Load actually detects that a restore failed, since ControlOutcome's restore variant carries no failure info. It seems like it would need to observe the kernel's fault state through something like PresentationClock/ClockView rather than getting failure info directly from the outcome itself.

So the fix is to add a LoadResult to the restore ControlOutcome with ok flag, fail_phase, fail_block_id, fail_code, and verdict fields as a foundation ask for ADR-0002. I'm also noting that recovery from FAULTED works by calling request_restore again on a previous generation, and that the kernel handles missing persist blocks generically by defaulting them rather than relying solely on Save/Load's pre-check.

Then I'm working through unknown-block handling: payload entries that reference non-persist blocks or PROFILE blocks during in-session restore should likely also trigger RESTORE_UNKNOWN_BLOCK, since they aren't restorable in that pass. I'm also checking how kernel.clock restore handles tick_rate mismatches, tracing through ADR-0005/0006/0002 for the TICK_RATE_MISMATCH description.

I'm deciding the kernel.clock payload entry should include T, world_seed, and tick_rate together, even though ADR-0006 §3.6 doesn't explicitly list tick_rate there — I'll flag this as an open question for the foundation to confirm. I also need to handle the restore_epoch overflow check and figure out how the pre-check step (faulting LOADING with pre-restore state intact) interacts with queue flushing before any restore() call happens.

Looking at the GDD's state table, a pre-check failure during LOADING transitions to FAULTED even though prior state is preserved, which seems odd but is recoverable since the registry stays valid — another request_restore or new_game could pull it out. I'm weighing whether this contradicts an alternative design where pre-check failure just gets refused/ignored and the kernel stays in its prior state, but that would conflict with the binding GDD table, so I need to treat FAULTED as the correct outcome here.

Now I'm working out the two-phase restore sequence as ordered stages: S0 handles entry (flushing the queue, installing the clock with world seed and restore epoch, checking registry validity), S1 is the pure pre-check that leaves state untouched, and S2 is the actual restore phase walking the DAG in order — restoring each persisted block's data if present or defaulting it if absent, and for new games, running every block's default_state first before chaining into init_world calls in DAG order under one scope.

I'm sorting out which blocks actually own an init_world — it looks like only Web Map does at MVP, orchestrating Layout's build_section, Emitter instantiation, Interaction's sync and placement, and Suit's seat defaults, all with its own internal fixed order. Then S3 runs post_restore per block in DAG order, S4 does the reproduction check with expected hash, S5 rebuilds bindings, and S6 exits by batching everything, setting load_seq, snapping the baseline, and transitioning to RUNNING.

For a fresh game the flow differs: default_state runs for every block in DAG order, then init_world runs under one INIT scope, followed by post_restore, binding rebuild, and exit. I also need to confirm the hash check occurs right after the last post_restore and rebuild happens after that check, per the kernel spec.

I'm mapping out a failure semantics table — for each stage, what can fail, the error code domain, what state the world ends up in, and how Save/Load should respond. Failures get attributed via a LoadFailure record capturing stage, block_id, code, and detail, with the kernel writing out diagnostics; there's no automatic revert. For the dead-end guard, I'm working through ADR-0011's requirement that a faulted LOADING state never lets play begin with a restored world — meaning the kernel must refuse ticks, reject commands, block snapshotting over an existing save, and withhold the ALL batch while load_seq stays unincremented and the presentation clock reflects the fault.

Partially restored blocks keep their data, but the FAULTED kernel state blocks any stepping; the only way out is request_restore or new_game, both of which rebuild every WORLD block from scratch so stale partial data can't leak forward, since each restore pass fully replaces every WORLD block and reruns post_restore on all derived caches. For presentation, since no ALL batch is delivered during FAULTED, the pipeline just shows an error screen rather than trying to build a world view from half-restored data.

I'm also working out a read-access rule for restore passes: during restore(X), a block may only read its own payload plus "restore-stable" views of predecessor blocks that are tagged as safe to read mid-restore, while post_restore(X) can read persisted state from any block but derived state only from blocks whose post_restore has already run earlier in the DAG. Since the kernel can't enforce this access rule directly, I'm proposing it be enforced via a lint pack — naming it RESTORE-ORDER RO-01 through RO-06 as new validation IDs under ADR-0010 rather than reusing existing numbering.

For verification, I land on an order-invariance test: run restore plus several random linear extensions of the DAG (worst-case orderings and seeded shuffles), then execute 60 ticks after each and compare the state_hash trace across all orders — this is the real equivalence check rather than trying to build a general derived-state digest. I'm also starting to sketch RestoreVerifier invariant functions with IDs, starting with the Layout block's graph-related checks.

For the Assembly block's invariants, I need to figure out where the verifier code actually lives versus which ADR owns the policy — concluding the implementation sits in assembly_verifier.gd while ADR-0016 owns the policy of when verifiers run, the registry of verifier IDs per block, and the fault-code naming scheme, with ADR-0021 owning the runtime "release subset after apply" behavior that calls the same functions. I'm designing the verifier API signature that takes views, a subset mask, and an output report, returning a packed result code.

Now I'm reasoning about fault code naming for restore verifiers: rather than one generic invariant code, I'll use per-invariant codes like domain-specific restore codes so first failures are cheap to identify, while leaving the actual table definition to ADR-0021 since that's Assembly's domain. I'm settling on a naming convention distinguishing restore-stage faults from post-restore verification faults, both namespaced under the owning domain, with the kernel layering on a load-stage marker.

Verification across verifiers follows the DAG order of owning blocks, and since each pass stops at the first fault deterministically, the same corrupted save always produces the same failing block and code -- which is exactly what makes large-scale fuzz testing tractable. Now I'm working through the binding rebuild details, defining the binding_source callable's payload as a flat PackedInt64Array of player/entity ID pairs in ascending order to avoid nested array allocations, with the kernel validating even length, strict ordering, no duplicates, and valid player seat ranges.

I'm also reasoning about edge cases: whether an unseated player_id in a binding should be an error or just a corruption signal (deciding it's valid as long as player_id ≥ 1, otherwise faulting with a PLAYER_RANGE detail), confirming that reading from sources is safe since it happens after all post_restore and K-4 steps, and defining the conflict rule where duplicate or conflicting bindings trigger a BINDING_REBUILD_CONFLICT fault, distinguishing conflict-type faults from source-fault-type faults via a detail reason field.

Rebuild order should follow ascending block_id per TR-cmd-013, which matters only for determinism of which conflict gets reported first since the result itself is order-independent. I'm also deciding that half (b) bindings must be cleared at entry to LOADING, not just rebuilt at the end, to prevent stale bindings from authorizing commands during a failed pass, and confirming via TR-saveload-037 that nothing binding-related is persisted in the save payload since bindings are always rebuilt fresh.

Now I'm tracing how seat binding sources get registered — they're declared at BOOTING through the block descriptor's binding_source field wrapping seat_bindings(), not through separate registration, and confirming the Controller isn't a binding source since it resolves entity ids via Body rather than owning them. I'm also checking that Body's post_restore explicitly doesn't rebuild kernel seat bindings per TR-shipbody-010, keeping that rebuild strictly kernel-owned, and noting BINDING_DRIFT handling after body-changing applies is already covered by ADR-0002 so it's not something I need to resolve here.

Next I'm working through TR-cmd-037: init_world runs once in a shared INIT scope after default_state is applied to all blocks in DAG order, and this only happens on NEW_GAME loads — never during RESTORE — which I can verify with a test asserting init_world's call counter stays zero on restore. A fault during init_world should close the INIT scope and transition the world to FAULTED, and new-game worlds should pass through the same post_restore verifiers as restored ones, giving a consistency guarantee that a freshly built world satisfies the same invariants.

Then I'm designing the restore-idempotence harness for TR-saveload-034: a generic test that takes every persisted block through snapshot → encode → decode → restore → snapshot, using per-block fixture factories that generate EMPTY, TYPICAL, and EXTREME payloads (covering caps and edge cases) via seeded RNG.

For REBASE_BLOCKS, I'm deciding this should be a committed constant array of block identifiers in the save module, with each entry annotated by owning ADR and intended removal point in a test-side data file; CI then enforces that idempotent blocks aren't stubbornly listed, non-idempotent blocks aren't missing, and the list empties out entirely by the first external build, gated on the same SHIPPED flag used for ID ledger freezing. At MVP, the interim list includes interaction.state, since post_restore currently drops channels, an open question I'm flagging as OQ-39.

Checking each candidate block, layout.state only needs a hash rewrite when geometry has drifted, not generally; assembly.state is already idempotent since snapshot() writes every seat's pending as NONE; controller.state normalizes during snapshot per PC-17 so it's idempotent too. That leaves interaction.state as the sole interim member of REBASE_BLOCKS.

I'm cross-checking this against the TR-interact-016 spec describing what post_restore drops (in-progress channels, door attempts, last_result) and resolves (RESERVED parts), concluding that if snapshot time is already doing the dropping, the restore-side drop effectively becomes a no-op on an already-normalized payload.

Since redefining Interaction's normalization behavior properly belongs to ADR-0020, but ADR-0016 is responsible for the post_restore write policy itself, I'll settle this by declaring Interaction's current post_restore normalization an interim exception under REBASE_BLOCKS, with the exit path being snapshot-time normalization that ADR-0020 must finalize before any external build — this avoids preempting Interaction's design while still unblocking progress.
